claims.text: The dominant tribo-corrosion degradation mechanism in high-entropy alloys is a synergistic cycle involving passive-film removal, corrosion, and further wear.
Mechanical wear repeatedly removes the protective passive oxide film.
Removal of the passive film exposes reactive metal surfaces that undergo accelerated localized corrosion.
Corrosion weakens the surface structure and thereby increases susceptibility to subsequent wear.
The baseline alloy has a well-developed, thermally stable passive oxide film.
The integrity and thickness of the passive oxide film mediate the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
The passive film normally limits metal dissolution.
Fresh bare metal produced by film removal is highly susceptible to localized corrosion.
Corrosion directly contributes to material loss.
Corrosion-induced microstructural deterioration reduces resistance to mechanical wear.
Feedback between film removal, corrosion, and surface weakening accelerates degradation beyond the additive effects of isolated wear and isolated corrosion.
Total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion will be significantly greater than the sum of degradation measured under isolated wear and isolated corrosion.
The wear component of degradation will be enhanced during the combined test relative to isolated wear.
The corrosion component of degradation will be enhanced during the combined test relative to isolated corrosion.
The passive film is disrupted less frequently under the isolated wear or isolated corrosion baselines than under simultaneous tribo-corrosion.
The proposed mechanism should apply when a stable passive oxide film forms and is important for corrosion resistance.
The predicted synergy may fail when the passive film is inherently unstable, repassivates extremely rapidly, or is not robust.
Thickening or stabilizing the passive film should reduce combined tribo-corrosion degradation and mitigate the synergistic effect.
